911.title: Gold on the Harmandir
911.hook: he covers the Harmandir in gilded copper and marble, and it becomes the Golden Temple
911.howItsDone: Sikhs visit the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, walk around the pool, listen to kirtan and serve in the langar; the gilded upper walls date from Maharaja Ranjit Singh's time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sarkar-e-Khalsa: a kingdom named for the Khalsa, with coins in the Gurus' names. Your line was the khalsa's rule. Whose name did you say out loud? Day nine hundred eleven.

Early morning at Amritsar. Mist on the water, the sound of kirtan carrying across the pool, and in the middle of it all a building that catches the first light and throws it back gold. People photograph that glow from every side of the pool. But the building wasn't always gold. This path has watched it rise, be desecrated, be blown up, and be rebuilt by the misls with plain hands and hard work. Today, someone covers it in light. Today: gold on the Harmandir.
screen: `MIST ON THE POOL AT DAWN.` → `A BUILDING THAT GLOWS.` → `IT WASN'T ALWAYS GOLD.`

segments.voice: Begin with what the building already was. The Harmandir Sahib, also called Darbar Sahib, the court of the Lord. Guru Arjan built it in the middle of the pool at Amritsar and placed the scripture inside. Tradition loves one detail: it has doors on every side, open to anyone from any direction. Then the hard years. The Harmandir was attacked and destroyed more than once, and the misls rebuilt it. That's where this path has been for a long stretch. Now Ranjit Singh. With a kingdom behind him, he gave the Harmandir its gold. The upper part of the building was covered with copper plates, and the copper was gilded, covered in a skin of gold. The lower walls were faced with marble, inlaid with stones and flower patterns. Craftsmen worked on it a long time. And slowly the building that Sikhs called the Harmandir became the one the world calls the Golden Temple. Here's what matters. He didn't build a new temple of his own. He took the Gurus' house, built by Guru Arjan, rebuilt by ordinary Sikhs, and gilded it. Once more, the king's wealth pointed past the king. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a hymn of Guru Arjan says that God himself stood up to finish the work of the saints, and tradition links it to the finishing of the pool. It is still sung when a piece of work is finished. The gold says the same thing in metal: this work is the Guru's, and the best we have belongs here.

segments.voice: Two minutes of polishing. If you can, pick up one small thing near you that you love but have let go dull: a ring, a frame, a pair of shoes, a window, a cup. Take a cloth, or your sleeve. Polish it slowly, with care, as if it belonged to someone you honor. If there's nothing to hand, polish it in your mind. Watch the shine come back. Notice your hands while they work. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Gold on the Harmandir. Gilded copper above, marble below, given by Ranjit Singh to the house Guru Arjan built. Today's word.
Your line: gold for the guru. Today, give your best effort to one ordinary thing that belongs to someone else, and don't sign your name to it. Day nine hundred eleven.

912.title: A river for a border, 1809
912.hook: a treaty with the British fixes the Sutlej as a boundary
912.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the treaty of Amritsar, which made the Sutlej the line between Ranjit Singh's kingdom and the British, and santokh, contentment, is named among the virtues in Sikh teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gold on the Harmandir: copper and marble and light, given to the Gurus' house. Your line was gold for the guru. What did you give your best to? Day nine hundred twelve.

Riders on one bank, the young Maharaja's. On the other bank, the chiefs who live to the south, nervous, looking over their shoulders. Between them, a wide brown river carrying snowmelt down from the mountains: the Sutlej. And behind them, a new power that has been moving up from the east: the British East India Company, with its own army and its own plans. Two growing powers, one river between them. Somebody is going to have to decide where one ends and the other begins. Today: a river for a border.
screen: `THE SUTLEJ RUNS BETWEEN.` → `NERVOUS CHIEFS TO THE SOUTH.` → `THE COMPANY MOVING UP.`

segments.voice: Three pieces to this. First, the pressure. Ranjit Singh had been crossing the Sutlej, drawing the chiefs south of it into his orbit. Some of those chiefs, including the Phulkian houses this path met earlier, turned to the British for protection. The Company sent an envoy, Charles Metcalfe, to the Maharaja's camp. Second, the bargain. The talks were tense, and the histories say they nearly broke more than once. In the end, at Amritsar, the two sides signed a treaty. The Sutlej would be the line. South of it, the British would protect the chiefs. North of it, the Maharaja was free to build his kingdom, and the Company would leave him alone. A river for a border. Third, what it cost and what it gave. It cost him a dream of ruling all the Sikh lands on both banks. That was a real loss. But it gave him peace on his eastern side, and he turned his energy north and west instead. And the histories say he kept his word: as long as he lived, he did not cross that line in force. In Japji, Guru Nanak says the bull that holds the earth in its place is dharma, born of compassion, and that contentment is the thread holding it steady. Santokh, contentment, is a Sikh virtue. Not giving up. Knowing where your line is, and letting that knowledge hold your world steady. A powerful man, drawing a line he could have pushed. That's the river line.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a line. Settle, and breathe. Think of one boundary in your life that matters: a friend's privacy, a coworker's time, a promise to yourself, a no someone said that you'd like to push on. Let it be a river, quiet and clear. You could cross it. You choose not to. Notice what that choice feels like in your body. Is there relief in it, or ache, or both? Let it be. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

913.title: A modern army
913.hook: he trains his army with European officers alongside Sikh generals
913.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember Ranjit Singh's army, trained in part by European officers and led by Sikh and Punjabi generals; the Guru Granth Sahib includes the hymns of the Gurus alongside those of saints from many backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a river for a border: the Sutlej, and a line he chose to keep. Your line was the river line. Which boundary did you let stand? Day nine hundred thirteen.

A parade ground outside Lahore, early morning. Rows of foot soldiers in matching jackets march in step to drums, turn on one command, and fire together. Across the field, the officers shout their orders in a mix of languages. Some of those officers are Punjabi chiefs whose families rode with the misls. And some have come from very far away, from France and Italy, men who learned soldiering in the wars of Europe. The misls fought as bands of horsemen. This is something new. Today: a modern army.
screen: `A PARADE GROUND OUTSIDE LAHORE.` → `DRUMS, DRILL AND VOLLEYS.` → `OFFICERS FROM FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the problem Ranjit Singh had. The misl way of fighting, fast riders striking and vanishing, had won the Punjab. But he had now seen the British across the river, with trained infantry and artillery that fought as one machine. He could ignore that, or learn from it. He learned. Ranjit Singh built new regiments of infantry and artillery drilled in the European way. To train them, he hired European officers, among them Jean-Baptiste Ventura and Jean-François Allard, who had served in Napoleon's armies. Accounts say he set them conditions: to respect Sikh ways in his lands, and, some sources say, not to eat beef or smoke. They taught drill and gunnery, and some led the new regiments on campaign. But the Maharaja kept command in his own hands, and his great campaigns were led by his own generals, Sikh and Punjabi. Now, a Sikh angle on this. Learning from outside is not new in Sikh history. The Guru Granth Sahib itself holds the hymns of the Gurus beside the hymns of saints from very different backgrounds: Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leatherworker, Namdev the tailor, and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. In Sikh telling, those words were placed in the scripture for what they say, not for where their writers came from. Guru Arjan gathered them into the book himself. Ranjit Singh's parade ground was a long way from the pages of the Granth. But the habit underneath was the same one: truth and skill can come through anyone. Learn from all.
screen: `THE MISLS FOUGHT AS RIDERS.` · `EUROPEAN DRILL, SIKH COMMAND.` · `CONDITIONS FOR THE OFFICERS.` · `SAINTS OF EVERY BACKGROUND IN THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM ALL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with an unlikely teacher. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you don't usually learn from: a person much younger, someone from a very different background, a coworker you find irritating, a stranger you overheard once. What do they know how to do that you don't? Let one skill or one way of seeing come to mind. Hold it with curiosity rather than judgment. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
A modern army. Ranjit Singh's regiments, drilled by European officers, commanded by his own generals, built by a ruler willing to learn. Today's word.
Your line: learn from all. Today, ask one person you'd normally overlook to show you how they do something. Then really watch. Day nine hundred thirteen.

914.title: Hari Singh Nalwa
914.hook: his great general held the north-west frontier and died at Jamrud
914.tomorrow: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
914.howItsDone: Sikhs tell stories of Hari Singh Nalwa as a general of great courage, and some connect his story with Kabir's verse about the true hero who never leaves the field.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a modern army: European drill, Sikh command, and a king willing to learn. Your line was learn from all. Who did you learn something from? Today, one of the generals who led that army. Day nine hundred fourteen.

Rocky hills. A narrow pass climbing west into the mountains: the Khyber. At its mouth stands a fort called Jamrud, and inside it a small garrison is waiting for a fight. Somewhere in the hills an army is coming down. The man responsible for this edge of the kingdom is a general whose name, the stories say, had become a word for nerve. When he falls, the fort still has to hold. Today: Hari Singh Nalwa.
screen: `THE MOUTH OF THE KHYBER.` → `A SMALL GARRISON AT JAMRUD.` → `A NAME THAT MEANT NERVE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Tradition explains Nalwa with a story: on a hunt, a tiger sprang at the young Hari Singh, and he fought it and killed it. Whether every detail is true or not, the name stuck to him like armor. Next, the job. Ranjit Singh's kingdom reached toward the mountains of the north-west, toward Peshawar and the Khyber. That edge was hard to hold: rough country, local powers with their own claims, and a kingdom in Kabul that claimed the same ground. Hari Singh Nalwa was sent to hold it. He governed, built forts, and kept the passes. Then Jamrud. Tradition tells it like this. An Afghan army came down to the fort. Hari Singh rode out to relieve it and was mortally wounded in the fighting. And as he lay dying, he asked his men to keep his death a secret, so that the defenders and the enemy alike would think he was still in command, until help could arrive. They did. Tradition says the fort held. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the saint Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the deen, a word some read as the helpless and some as the faith, and who would be cut to pieces before leaving the field. Some Sikhs hear that line in stories like this one. Notice what the story honors. Not glory, not the size of the battle. A man who stood at the edge so others could live behind it, and who even in dying thought about who would hold the line. The frontier held.

915.title: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
915.word: The Maharaja at the Akal Takht
915.hook: tradition says the Nihang leader Akali Phula Singh summoned Ranjit Singh to the Akal Takht for penance and he came humbly
915.howItsDone: Sikhs regard the Akal Takht in Amritsar as the seat from which the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account, and the story of Ranjit Singh accepting Akali Phula Singh's summons is told as an example that no Sikh stands above it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hari Singh Nalwa: a general at the mouth of the Khyber, holding the line even as he died. Your line was the frontier held. What line did you hold? Day nine hundred fifteen.

A message arrives at the palace in Lahore. It isn't from a rival king or the British. It comes from Amritsar, from the Akal Takht, and it is addressed to the Maharaja himself. It says, in effect: you have broken Sikh discipline. Come and answer for it. The man who sent it has no kingdom. He leads a band of Nihangs, fierce, plain-living Sikh warriors. The man receiving it rules the Punjab. Everyone at court waits to see what he'll do. Today: the Maharaja at the Akal Takht.
screen: `A SUMMONS FROM AMRITSAR.` → `ADDRESSED TO THE MAHARAJA.` → `SENT BY A MAN WITH NO KINGDOM.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The Akal Takht, the throne of the Timeless One, stands facing the Harmandir across the walkway at Amritsar. Sikh tradition says Guru Hargobind raised it as the seat where the community's worldly affairs would be decided before God. From there, the Khalsa can call any Sikh to account. Any Sikh. Next, the man. Akali Phula Singh was a Nihang leader, a warrior known for his courage and his strictness, and tradition remembers him serving at the Akal Takht. He fought in Ranjit Singh's campaigns. But when, as the story goes, the Maharaja's own conduct broke Sikh discipline, Phula Singh did not look away. He summoned him. Then, the moment. Tradition says Ranjit Singh came, not with soldiers, but on foot, with folded hands. He admitted the wrong. He accepted the punishment given, and by the common telling, it was a flogging. He bared his back. And the gathered Sikhs, seeing the ruler of the Punjab standing there with his head bowed, were so moved that they cried out for mercy, and the punishment was set aside for a fine. Notice who's above whom. In the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the king spoke of serving the Khalsa. Here, for one morning, it wasn't just a phrase. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue. The Maharaja who laughed about his one eye could also bow his head. Even the king bowed.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a correction. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone told you that you'd got something wrong, and they were right. Maybe you took it well. Maybe you didn't. Let the memory come without flinching. Now picture yourself receiving it again, this time with your hands open and your head a little lowered. Not crushed. Just willing. Notice what loosens when you stop defending. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Maharaja at the Akal Takht. Summoned by Akali Phula Singh, he came humbly and accepted the Khalsa's correction. Today's word.

916.title: Multan, 1818
916.hook: the city of saints and heat joins the kingdom
916.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the janamsakhi story of Guru Nanak's jasmine flower on the bowl of milk at Multan, and Sikh histories remember the siege of Multan and the courage of its governor, Nawab Muzaffar Khan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maharaja at the Akal Takht: summoned, he came on foot and bowed his head. Your line was even the king bowed. Did someone correct you, and how did you answer? Day nine hundred sixteen.

Heat that hits like an open oven door. Dust in the air, the sun white overhead, and rising out of the haze, the domes of shrines, glazed in blue and white tiles. Multan, far down in the south of the Punjab. Some call it a city of saints, for its Sufi shrines, and a city of heat, for reasons you can feel on your skin. It has a fort, and a governor inside it who has no intention of giving it up. Today: Multan.
screen: `HEAT LIKE AN OVEN DOOR.` → `BLUE-TILED SHRINES IN THE HAZE.` → `A GOVERNOR IN THE FORT.`

segments.voice: Start long before the kingdom. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak coming to Multan on his travels. The janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, tell it this way. The holy men of the city, hearing a new teacher had arrived, sent him a bowl of milk filled to the brim. The message was polite and clear: this city is already full of saints; there's no room for one more. Guru Nanak took a small jasmine flower and laid it on the milk. It floated. Not a drop spilled. His answer: I won't take your room. I'll only add a fragrance. Now the siege. Ranjit Singh had tried for Multan before and been turned back. This time his army came to stay, with heavy guns, and the fort was surrounded through the heat. Its governor, Nawab Muzaffar Khan, refused to surrender. Tradition says that when the walls were finally breached, he came out sword in hand with his sons beside him and fought until he fell. Sikh accounts remember his courage with respect. An enemy can be honored. Then the city joins. Multan, with its shrines and its markets and its long road to the south, became part of the kingdom, and the kingdom now reached deep into the south of the Punjab. Put the two stories side by side. A flower that doesn't spill the milk, and a governor who wouldn't yield. Multan joins, but the city of saints stays a city of saints.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK, FULL TO THE BRIM.` · `GURU NANAK'S JASMINE FLOWER.` · `A GOVERNOR WHO FOUGHT TO THE END.` · `THE CITY JOINS THE KINGDOM.` · then, large: `MULTAN JOINS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes somewhere hot. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind travel to the hottest place you've ever stood: a summer street, a kitchen in July, a beach at noon. Feel the heat on your skin, the light pressing on your eyelids, the slowness it brings. Then let a small cool thing arrive: a breeze, a cup of water, a white flower floating on milk. Let your breath slow around it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Multan. The city of saints and heat, where Guru Nanak laid a flower on the milk, and which joined Ranjit Singh's kingdom after a hard siege. Today's word.

917.title: Kashmir, 1819
917.hook: the valley comes under Sikh rule
917.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Kashmir campaign in histories of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign, where it is told as one of the conquests that took the kingdom into the mountains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan: the hot city of saints, and your line was multan joins. Which full room did you walk into, and what small thing did you add? Today we climb out of the plains, and close the week. Day nine hundred seventeen.

Snow on the passes. A lake with houseboats. Fields of saffron, and shawls so fine, the old stories say, that one could be drawn through a ring. That's Kashmir, the valley ringed by mountains to the north of the Punjab. For a long time it had been ruled from far away, by governors sent from Kabul. Then, in the way Sikh histories tell it, an army came up the mountain roads from Lahore, dragging its guns behind it. Today: Kashmir.
screen: `SNOW, SAFFRON, SHAWLS.` → `A VALLEY RULED FROM FAR AWAY.` → `AN ARMY FROM LAHORE.`

segments.voice: Start with the road. Getting an army into Kashmir meant hauling men and guns over high passes, and Sikh histories remember that an earlier try had failed. So the second try was planned with care. The Maharaja sent his general, Misr Diwan Chand, a Hindu officer who had risen in his service, with Sikh commanders beside him. The army crossed the mountains and met the Afghan governor's forces, and the valley was won. Second, the change at the top. Kashmir had been held for the kings in Kabul. Now its governors were named in Lahore, by the Maharaja of the Khalsa's kingdom. Histories tell of Kashmir's shawls and saffron reaching the Lahore court, and of the Maharaja's love of fine Kashmiri things. Third, the honest part. Ruling a valley is harder than winning one. Some governors sent from Lahore are remembered well, some less so, and Kashmiri memory of these years is mixed. A kingdom can take a beautiful place and still govern it unevenly. That belongs in the story too. And fourth, the week. Look back at the road we've walked these seven days: gold laid on the Harmandir, a river fixed as a border, an army trained by teachers from many lands, a general who held the frontier, a Maharaja who bowed to correction at the Akal Takht, Multan in the heat. And now the valley, high and cool, at the top of the map. Day by day, the story has followed a city becoming a country. The valley is where the map reached the snow.
screen: `A HARD ROAD OVER THE PASSES.` · `GOVERNORS NAMED IN LAHORE.` · `WINNING IS EASIER THAN RULING.` · `A WEEK OF A GROWING KINGDOM.` · then, large: `THE VALLEY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in a valley. Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Picture mountains on every side of you, close and high, with snow on their tops. The air is cold and clean. Down where you are, it's sheltered and green, and water moves somewhere nearby. Breathe in the cold air. Breathe out slowly. Let the mountains hold the noise of the week outside. If you pray, you can say Waheguru quietly on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Kashmir. The valley of snow, saffron and shawls, won by an army that crossed the passes from Lahore, and governed from there. Today's word.
Your line: the valley. Today, find one sheltered place, a quiet corner, a short walk, five minutes in a parked car, and rest there before you go back out. Day nine hundred seventeen.
